title: Build.io and Stacksync: The Complete Heroku Migration Stack
summary: Build.io moves your apps and platform off Heroku. Stacksync replaces Heroku Connect with real-time, two-way Salesforce to Postgres sync. Here is how they fit.
body_markdown:
## What is the complete Heroku migration stack?


A complete Heroku exit has two parts: moving the application and platform, and replacing Heroku Connect.[Build.io](https://www.build.io/) moves apps off Heroku, including hosting, dynos, Postgres, add-ons and pipelines. Stacksync replaces Heroku Connect with real-time, two-way sync between Salesforce and Postgres, so your app keeps the tables it depends on.


Together they cover the full path out of Heroku. Teams do not have to choose between rebuilding their data integration and staying on a platform they have decided to leave.


## Why does a Heroku exit have two separate parts?


Heroku is two different things to most Salesforce-connected teams. It is a place to run code: web and worker dynos, a managed Postgres database, add-ons for logging and caching, and pipelines for promoting builds. It is also, through Heroku Connect, the bridge that keeps Salesforce records mirrored into Postgres tables and writes changes back.


These layers fail in different ways during a migration. If the app moves but the sync does not, the new environment has a database that no longer receives Salesforce updates. If the sync is ripped out first, the app loses its data before it has anywhere to go. Treating them as one project with two owners is the safer approach.


Heroku has said the platform is in sustaining engineering. For teams that rely on Heroku Connect, that makes the sync a long-term decision rather than a setting to leave alone. Planning the move now, on your own schedule, is easier than reacting to a change later.


Moving from Heroku Connect to Stacksync during a Heroku migration


## Who handles what in a Build.io and Stacksync migration?


The split is simple. Build.io owns the platform. Stacksync owns the data sync between your business systems and Postgres.


Heroku component What it does today Who replaces it


App hosting and dynos Runs web and worker processes Build.io


Heroku Postgres Stores application data, including Heroku Connect tables Build.io (platform move)


Add-ons Logging, caching, scheduling and other services Build.io


Pipelines Promote builds from staging to production Build.io


Heroku Connect Syncs Salesforce objects to and from Postgres tables Stacksync


Other CRM and ERP integrations Custom scripts or third-party connectors Stacksync (HubSpot, NetSuite and more)


Stacksync connects to Postgres wherever it ends up. That means the sync can be configured against the database Build.io stands up, using the same Salesforce objects and the same table names. See the[Salesforce connector](https://www.stacksync.com/connectors/salesforce) for the objects and sync behavior supported.


## What stays the same for your application?


The main concern teams raise about leaving Heroku Connect is the fear of rewriting the app. The application code reads and writes Postgres tables, not Heroku Connect itself. If the replacement sync keeps those tables in place, the code does not need to know anything changed.


-


The same Salesforce objects are synced.


-


The same Postgres tables and columns are populated.


-


Application queries and writes keep working against those tables.


-


Changes made in Postgres flow back to Salesforce, and changes in Salesforce flow to Postgres.


The principle


Same objects, same tables. Only the sync layer changes.
